lessons.title: Unit 8 Summary - Length, Mass and Capacity
lessons.notes_html:
This summary gathers the main facts of Unit 8: Length, Mass and Capacity. Revise these points before a test.

Formula: 1 km = 1000 m.

Formula: 1 m = 100 cm.

Formula: 1 cm = 10 mm.

Formula: 1 kg = 1000 g.

Formula: 1 litre = 1000 ml.

Key Points

  • Formula: 1 km = 1000 m; 1 m = 100 cm; 1 cm = 10 mm.
  • Formula: 1 kg = 1000 g.
  • Formula: 1 litre = 1000 ml.
  • Larger unit to smaller unit: multiply. Smaller unit to larger unit: divide.
  • Change measures to the same unit before adding or subtracting.

mcqs.q: What is the formula for changing kilometres into metres?
mcqs.why: Step 1: The summary gives the formula 1 km = 1000 m. Step 2: So each kilometre is equal to one thousand metres.

mcqs.q: What is the formula for changing metres into centimetres?
mcqs.why: Step 1: The summary gives the formula 1 m = 100 cm. Step 2: So each metre is equal to one hundred centimetres.

mcqs.q: What is the formula for changing centimetres into millimetres?
mcqs.why: Step 1: The summary gives the formula 1 cm = 10 mm. Step 2: So each centimetre is equal to ten millimetres.

mcqs.q: What is the formula for changing kilograms into grams?
mcqs.why: Step 1: The summary gives the formula 1 kg = 1000 g. Step 2: So each kilogram is equal to one thousand grams.

mcqs.q: What is the formula for changing litres into millilitres?
mcqs.why: Step 1: The summary gives the formula 1 litre = 1000 ml. Step 2: So each litre is equal to one thousand millilitres.

mcqs.q: To change a larger unit into a smaller unit, what do you do?
mcqs.why: Step 1: The key points say larger unit to smaller unit: multiply. Step 2: Multiplying gives the larger count needed in the smaller unit.

mcqs.q: To change a smaller unit into a larger unit, what do you do?
mcqs.why: Step 1: The key points say smaller unit to larger unit: divide. Step 2: Dividing gives the smaller count needed in the larger unit.

mcqs.q: What must you do before adding or subtracting measures?
options: Change them to the same unit
mcqs.why: Step 1: The key points say to change measures to the same unit before adding or subtracting. Step 2: Only then are the numbers added or subtracted correctly.

mcqs.q: Which list gives all three length formulas from the summary?
mcqs.why: Step 1: The summary lists the length formulas together. Step 2: They are 1 km = 1000 m, 1 m = 100 cm and 1 cm = 10 mm.

mcqs.q: Which measure is about capacity in the Unit 8 summary?
mcqs.why: Step 1: The summary gives the formula 1 litre = 1000 ml for capacity. Step 2: So litre and millilitre are the capacity units in the summary.

lessons.title: Unit 9 Overview - Time and Date (textbook page 105)
lessons.notes_html:
Learning Outcomes

Read and write time from digital and analogue clocks in 12-hour and 24-hour format. Convert larger units to smaller units of time (hours, minutes, seconds, years, months, weeks and days). Calculate the duration of events using start time and end time. Add, subtract and convert measures of time to solve real-life word problems. Read days and dates from the calendar.

Reading clocks, 12-hour and 24-hour time, converting hours, minutes and seconds, years, months, weeks and days, and finding elapsed time.

mcqs.q: Which clock formats does Unit 9 teach you to read and write?
mcqs.why: Step 1: The outcomes say to read and write time from digital and analogue clocks in 12-hour and 24-hour format. Step 2: Both formats are covered in Unit 9.

mcqs.q: Which time units are named for conversion in Unit 9?
options: Hours, minutes, seconds, years, months, weeks and days
mcqs.why: Step 1: The outcomes list converting hours, minutes, seconds, years, months, weeks and days. Step 2: These are the time units converted from larger to smaller in Unit 9.

mcqs.q: How do you calculate the duration of an event?
options: By using only the start time
By using only the end time
By adding the date to the time
Using its start time and end time
mcqs.why: Step 1: The outcomes say to calculate the duration of events using start time and end time. Step 2: The duration is the time between those two times.

mcqs.q: What does Unit 9 teach you to read from the calendar?
mcqs.why: Step 1: The outcomes say to read days and dates from the calendar. Step 2: The calendar is used for days and dates in Unit 9.

mcqs.q: What kind of problems does Unit 9 solve with time measures?
mcqs.why: Step 1: The outcomes say to add, subtract and convert measures of time to solve real-life word problems. Step 2: So time work in Unit 9 is applied to real-life word problems.

mcqs.q: In Unit 9, conversions of time go in which direction?
options: From smaller units to larger units only
From larger units to smaller units
mcqs.why: Step 1: The outcomes say to convert larger units to smaller units of time. Step 2: For example, hours are changed into minutes, a smaller unit.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a topic listed for Unit 9?
mcqs.why: Step 1: The overview lists finding elapsed time among the Unit 9 topics. Step 2: Elapsed time is the time that passes between a start and an end.

mcqs.q: Which two kinds of clocks are named in Unit 9?
mcqs.why: Step 1: The outcomes mention reading time from digital and analogue clocks. Step 2: Both clock kinds are used to practise reading and writing time.

mcqs.q: Which topic connects 12-hour time with its other format in Unit 9?
mcqs.why: Step 1: The overview lists 12-hour and 24-hour time as a topic. Step 2: This topic covers writing the same time in both formats.

mcqs.q: Which set of units is grouped together in the Unit 9 overview for converting?
mcqs.why: Step 1: The overview lists converting hours, minutes and seconds together. Step 2: These are the clock-time units converted in Unit 9.

lessons.title: Exercise 9.1
lessons.notes_html:
Method: On an analogue clock the short hand shows the hour and the long hand shows the minutes. Formula: Minutes shown = number on the clock x 5. In 12-hour time, a.m. is from midnight to noon and p.m. is from noon to midnight.

Exercise 9.1 - Worked item

(i) 7:15, which is 15 minutes past 7.

(ii) 3:30, which is half past 3.

(iii) 9:25, which is 25 minutes past 9.

(iv) 11:15, which is 15 minutes past 11.

(v) 8:10, which is 10 minutes past 8.

(vi) 1:45, which is 45 minutes past 1. Note: the times are given in hours and minutes, the form used in the lesson examples; seconds on the red second hand are not read here.

mcqs.q: On an analogue clock, what does the short hand show?
mcqs.why: Step 1: The method says the short hand shows the hour. Step 2: The long hand shows the minutes, so the short hand must be read for the hour.

mcqs.q: On an analogue clock, what does the long hand show?
mcqs.why: Step 1: The method says the long hand shows the minutes. Step 2: The short hand shows the hour, so the long hand must be read for the minutes.

mcqs.q: How do you work out the minutes shown on an analogue clock?
mcqs.why: Step 1: The formula says minutes shown = number on the clock x 5. Step 2: Multiply the number the long hand points to by 5 to get the minutes.

mcqs.q: What does a.m. mean in 12-hour time?
mcqs.why: Step 1: The method says a.m. is from midnight to noon. Step 2: So morning times before noon are written with a.m.

mcqs.q: What does p.m. mean in 12-hour time?
mcqs.why: Step 1: The method says p.m. is from noon to midnight. Step 2: So afternoon and evening times are written with p.m.

mcqs.q: How is the time 7:15 described in words in the worked item?
mcqs.why: Step 1: The worked item gives 7:15, which is 15 minutes past 7. Step 2: The minutes part, 15, tells how many minutes past the hour 7 it is.

mcqs.q: How is the time 3:30 described in words in the worked item?
mcqs.why: Step 1: The worked item gives 3:30, which is half past 3. Step 2: 30 minutes is half of an hour, so 3:30 is called half past 3.

mcqs.q: What time is described as 25 minutes past 9?
mcqs.why: Step 1: The worked item gives 9:25, which is 25 minutes past 9. Step 2: The hour is 9 and the minutes are 25, written as 9:25.

mcqs.q: What time is described as 10 minutes past 8?
mcqs.why: Step 1: The worked item gives 8:10, which is 10 minutes past 8. Step 2: The hour is 8 and the minutes are 10, written as 8:10.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 9.1, are the seconds on the red second hand read?
options: No, seconds are not read here

lessons.title: Exercise 9.3

mcqs.q: Convert 45 minutes to seconds.

mcqs.q: To change a smaller time unit back into a larger unit, what do you do?

mcqs.q: Convert 7 hours to minutes.

lessons.title: Exercise 9.5
lessons.notes_html:
Method: Subtract hours from hours and minutes from minutes. If the minutes cannot be subtracted, borrow 1 hour as 60 minutes first. Note: 3 minutes 10 seconds = 190 seconds, not 100 seconds as the printed key says; the worked items use the correct value.

Exercise 9.5 - Item 1: Find the time from 2:30 p.m. to 8:15 p.m

Step 1: From 2:30 p.m. to 8:30 p.m. is 6 hours.

Step 2: 8:15 p.m. is 15 minutes earlier, so subtract 15 minutes: 6 hours - 15 minutes = 5 hours 45 minutes.

Answer: 2:30 p.m. to 8:15 p.m. =5 hours 45 minutes.

Exercise 9.5 - Item 2: Find the time from 2:40 p.m. to 3:25 p.m

Step 1: From 2:40 p.m. to 3:00 p.m. is 20 minutes.

Step 2: From 3:00 p.m. to 3:25 p.m. is 25 minutes.

Step 3: 20 + 25 = 45 minutes.

Answer: 2:40 p.m. to 3:25 p.m. =45 minutes.

Exercise 9.5 - Item 3(a): Find the time from 7:30 a.m. to 9:00 a.m

Step 1: From 7:30 a.m. to 9:00 a.m. is 1 hour 30 minutes.

Answer: 7:30 a.m. to 9:00 a.m. =1 hour 30 minutes.

Exercise 9.5 - Item 3(b): Find the time from 11:15 a.m. to 11:55 a.m

Step 1: 11:55 - 11:15 = 40 minutes.

Answer: 11:15 a.m. to 11:55 a.m. =40 minutes.

Exercise 9.5 - Item 4: It is 10:30 p.m. What will the time be after 1 hour 40 minutes

Step 1: 10:30 p.m. + 1 hour = 11:30 p.m.

Step 2: 11:30 p.m. + 40 minutes = 12:10 a.m. (past midnight).

Answer: After 1 hour 40 minutes it will be 12:10 a.m.

Exercise 9.5 - Item 5: Find the time from 5 p.m. to 8:30 p.m

Step 1: From 5 p.m. to 8 p.m. is 3 hours, plus 30 minutes = 3 hours 30 minutes.

Answer: 5 p.m. to 8:30 p.m. =3 hours 30 minutes.

mcqs.q: Find the time from 2:30 p.m. to 8:15 p.m.
mcqs.why: Step 1: From 2:30 p.m. to 8:30 p.m. is 6 hours. Step 2: 8:15 p.m. is 15 minutes earlier, so 6 hours - 15 minutes = 5 hours 45 minutes.

mcqs.q: Find the time from 2:40 p.m. to 3:25 p.m.
mcqs.why: Step 1: From 2:40 p.m. to 3:00 p.m. is 20 minutes. Step 2: From 3:00 p.m. to 3:25 p.m. is 25 minutes. Step 3: 20 + 25 = 45 minutes.

mcqs.q: Find the time from 7:30 a.m. to 9:00 a.m.
mcqs.why: Step 1: From 7:30 a.m. to 8:30 a.m. is 1 hour. Step 2: From 8:30 a.m. to 9:00 a.m. is 30 minutes. Step 3: Total is 1 hour 30 minutes.

mcqs.q: Find the time from 11:15 a.m. to 11:55 a.m.
mcqs.why: Step 1: Both times are in the same hour, so subtract the minutes: 55 - 15 = 40. Step 2: So the time from 11:15 a.m. to 11:55 a.m. is 40 minutes.

mcqs.q: It is 10:30 p.m. What will the time be after 1 hour 40 minutes?

mcqs.q: Find the time from 5 p.m. to 8:30 p.m.
mcqs.why: Step 1: From 5 p.m. to 8 p.m. is 3 hours. Step 2: Add the extra 30 minutes: 3 hours + 30 minutes = 3 hours 30 minutes.

mcqs.q: When subtracting times, what do you do if the minutes cannot be subtracted?
mcqs.why: Step 1: The method says subtract hours from hours and minutes from minutes. Step 2: If the minutes cannot be subtracted, borrow 1 hour as 60 minutes first.

mcqs.q: How many seconds are in 3 minutes 10 seconds?
mcqs.why: Step 1: 3 minutes = 3 x 60 = 180 seconds. Step 2: 180 + 10 = 190 seconds. The notes correct the printed key: it is 190 seconds, not 100 seconds.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 9.5, times are subtracted in which way?

mcqs.q: What is 60 minutes equal to, when borrowing in time subtraction?
mcqs.why: Step 1: The method uses the fact that 1 hour = 60 minutes. Step 2: So when borrowing, 1 hour is taken as 60 minutes and added to the minutes.

lessons.title: Exercise 9.6
lessons.notes_html:
Method: A calendar shows the days, weeks and months of a year. Formula: 1 week = 7 days. Formula: 1 year = 12 months. Count forward or backward carefully from the given date, month by month.

Exercise 9.6 - Item 1: 1 hour 20 minutes and 1 hour 10 minutes

Step 2: Add minutes: 20 + 10 = 30 minutes.

Answer: 1 hour 20 minutes + 1 hour 10 minutes =2 hours 30 minutes.

Exercise 9.6 - Item 2: A watch is 15 minutes fast and shows 3:25 p.m. What is the actual time

Answer: The actual time is 3:10 p.m.

Answer: 8 hours 30 minutes - 6 hours 15 minutes =2 hours 15 minutes longer.

mcqs.q: Add 40 minutes and 1 hour 10 minutes.
mcqs.why: Step 1: 1 hour 10 minutes = 70 minutes. Step 2: 40 + 70 = 110 minutes. Step 3: 110 minutes = 1 hour 50 minutes.

mcqs.q: Find the time from 13:00 to 14:20.

mcqs.q: One route takes 8 hours 30 minutes and another takes 6 hours 15 minutes. How much longer is the first route?

mcqs.q: How many days are in 1 week?

mcqs.q: How many months are in 1 year?

lessons.title: Unit 9 Summary - Time and Date
lessons.notes_html:
This summary gathers the main facts of Unit 9: Time and Date. Revise these points before a test.

Formula: 1 hour = 60 minutes.

Formula: 1 minute = 60 seconds.

Formula: 1 day = 24 hours.

Formula: 1 week = 7 days.

Key Points

  • Formula: 1 hour = 60 minutes; 1 minute = 60 seconds; 1 day = 24 hours; 1 week = 7 days.
  • a.m. is midnight to noon; p.m. is noon to midnight.
  • Formula: 24-hour time = 12-hour time + 12 hours for p.m. times.
  • Adding time: 60 minutes make 1 hour. Subtracting time: borrow 1 hour as 60 minutes.
  • 22:45 is 10:45 p.m. and 3 minutes 10 seconds is 190 seconds.

mcqs.q: How many minutes are in 1 hour?
mcqs.why: Step 1: The summary gives the formula 1 hour = 60 minutes. Step 2: So each hour contains sixty minutes.

mcqs.q: How many seconds are in 1 minute?
mcqs.why: Step 1: The summary gives the formula 1 minute = 60 seconds. Step 2: So each minute contains sixty seconds.

mcqs.q: How many hours are in 1 day?
mcqs.why: Step 1: The summary gives the formula 1 day = 24 hours. Step 2: So each day contains twenty-four hours.

mcqs.q: How many days are in 1 week?
mcqs.why: Step 1: The summary gives the formula 1 week = 7 days. Step 2: So each week contains seven days.

mcqs.q: In the summary, a.m. is the time from where to where?
mcqs.why: Step 1: The key points say a.m. is midnight to noon. Step 2: So times after midnight and before noon are written with a.m.

mcqs.q: In the summary, p.m. is the time from where to where?
mcqs.why: Step 1: The key points say p.m. is noon to midnight. Step 2: So times from noon onwards are written with p.m.

mcqs.q: How do you get 24-hour time from a p.m. time?
mcqs.why: Step 1: The formula says 24-hour time = 12-hour time + 12 hours for p.m. times. Step 2: Adding 12 hours converts the p.m. time.

mcqs.q: When adding time, what do 60 minutes make?
mcqs.why: Step 1: The key points say adding time: 60 minutes make 1 hour. Step 2: So minutes reaching 60 are regrouped as one extra hour.

mcqs.q: When subtracting time, how is 1 hour borrowed?
mcqs.why: Step 1: The key points say subtracting time: borrow 1 hour as 60 minutes. Step 2: This gives enough minutes to complete the subtraction.

mcqs.q: According to the summary, what is 22:45 in 12-hour time?
mcqs.why: Step 1: 22 - 12 = 10, and 22:45 is at night so it is p.m. Step 2: The summary confirms 22:45 is 10:45 p.m., and 3 minutes 10 seconds is 190 seconds.

lessons.title: Unit 10 Overview - Perimeter and Area (textbook page 115)
lessons.notes_html:
Learning Outcomes

Identify the units of measurement for perimeter and area. Differentiate between the perimeter and area of a square, a rectangle and a rectilinear shape. Apply formulas to find the perimeter and area of squares, rectangles and rectilinear shapes.

Perimeter is the distance around a shape. Area is the space inside a shape. For a rectangle: perimeter = 2 x (length + breadth), area = length x breadth. For a square: perimeter = 4 x side, area = side x side.

mcqs.q: What is perimeter?
options: The length of one side only
mcqs.why: The notes define perimeter as the distance around a shape, measured by going all the way round its edge.

mcqs.q: What is area?
options: The longest side of a shape
mcqs.why: The notes define area as the space inside a shape, which is different from the distance around it.

mcqs.q: What is the formula for the perimeter of a rectangle?
mcqs.why: Step 1: Perimeter of a rectangle = 2 x (length + breadth), as given in the Unit 10 overview notes.

mcqs.q: What is the formula for the area of a rectangle?
mcqs.why: Step 1: Area of a rectangle = length x breadth, as given in the Unit 10 overview notes for this lesson.

mcqs.q: What is the formula for the perimeter of a square?
mcqs.why: Step 1: Perimeter of a square = 4 x side, because a square has four equal sides added together.

mcqs.q: What is the formula for the area of a square?
mcqs.why: Step 1: Area of a square = side x side, as given in the Unit 10 overview notes for this lesson.

mcqs.q: Which shapes does Unit 10 teach you to find the perimeter and area of?
mcqs.why: The learning outcomes say to differentiate and apply formulas for squares, rectangles and rectilinear shapes.

mcqs.q: A rectangle has length 3 cm and breadth 2 cm. Using the overview formula, what is its perimeter?
mcqs.why: Step 1: Perimeter = 2 x (3 + 2) = 2 x 5 = 10 cm, using the rectangle perimeter formula from the notes.

mcqs.q: A square has side 4 cm. Using the overview formula, what is its area?
mcqs.why: Step 1: Area = side x side = 4 x 4 = 16 square cm, using the square area formula from the notes.

mcqs.q: How is perimeter different from area?
options: Perimeter is inside, area is around
Perimeter is around the shape, area is inside the shape
Both are measured only in metres
mcqs.why: The notes state perimeter is the distance around a shape while area is the space inside a shape.

lessons.title: Exercise 10.1
lessons.notes_html:
Method: Perimeter is the distance around a shape and area is the space inside it. Formula: Perimeter of a rectangle = 2 x (length + breadth). Formula: Area of a rectangle = length x breadth. Formula: Perimeter of a square = 4 x side. Formula: Area of a square = side x side. For a rectilinear shape, add all the side lengths for the perimeter, and split the shape into rectangles and add their areas for the area.

Exercise 10.1 - Item 1(i): A rectangle is 3 cm long and 2 cm wide. Find its perimeter and area

Formula: Perimeter of a rectangle = 2 x (length + breadth).

Formula: Area of a rectangle = length x breadth.

Step 1: Perimeter = 2 x (3 + 2) = 2 x 5 = 10 cm.

Step 2: Area = 3 x 2 = 6 square cm.

Answer: Perimeter = 10 cm, Area =6 cm squared.

Exercise 10.1 - Item 1(ii): A square has side 4 cm. Find its perimeter and area

Formula: Perimeter of a square = 4 x side.

Formula: Area of a square = side x side.

Step 1: Perimeter = 4 x 4 = 16 cm.

Step 2: Area = 4 x 4 = 16 square cm.

Answer: Perimeter = 16 cm, Area =16 cm squared.

Exercise 10.1 - Item 1(iii): A square has side 7 cm. Find its perimeter and area

Formula: Perimeter of a square = 4 x side.

Formula: Area of a square = side x side.

Step 1: Perimeter = 4 x 7 = 28 cm.

Step 2: Area = 7 x 7 = 49 square cm.

Answer: Perimeter = 28 cm, Area =49 cm squared.

Exercise 10.1 - Item 1(iv): A rectangle is 5 cm long and 3 cm wide. Find its perimeter and area

Formula: Perimeter of a rectangle = 2 x (length + breadth).

Formula: Area of a rectangle = length x breadth.

Step 1: Perimeter = 2 x (5 + 3) = 2 x 8 = 16 cm.

Step 2: Area = 5 x 3 = 15 square cm.

Answer: Perimeter = 16 cm, Area =15 cm squared.

Exercise 10.1 - Item 1(v): Find the perimeter and area of the rectilinear shape in the book (sides 3, 3, 3, 2, 2, 3, 2, 2 cm in order around the shape)

Formula: Perimeter of a rectangle = 2 x (length + breadth).

Formula: Area of a rectangle = length x breadth.

Step 1: Perimeter: add all eight sides: 3 + 3 + 3 + 2 + 2 + 3 + 2 + 2 = 20 cm.

Step 2: Area: split the shape into a 3 cm by 3 cm part (9 square cm) and a 2 cm by 3 cm part (6 square cm): 9 + 6 = 15 square cm.

Answer: Perimeter = 20 cm, Area =15 cm squared.

Exercise 10.1 - Item 2: A wall is 4 m long and 3 m wide. Find its perimeter and area

Step 1: Perimeter = 2 x (4 + 3) = 14 m.

Step 2: Area = 4 x 3 = 12 square m.

Answer: Perimeter = 14 m, Area =12 m squared.

Exercise 10.1 - Item 3: A square ground has side 8 cm. Find its perimeter and area

Formula: Perimeter of a square = 4 x side.

Formula: Area of a square = side x side.

Step 1: Perimeter = 4 x 8 = 32 cm.

Step 2: Area = 8 x 8 = 64 square cm.

Answer: Perimeter = 32 cm, Area =64 cm squared.

lessons.title: Unit 10 Summary - Perimeter and Area
lessons.notes_html:
This summary gathers the main facts of Unit 10: Perimeter and Area. Revise these points before a test.

Formula: Perimeter of a rectangle = 2 x (length + breadth).

Formula: Area of a rectangle = length x breadth.

Formula: Perimeter of a square = 4 x side.

Formula: Area of a square = side x side.

Key Points

  • Perimeter is the distance around a shape, measured in cm or m.
  • Area is the space inside a shape, measured in square units.
  • Formula: Perimeter of a rectangle = 2 x (length + breadth); Area = length x breadth.
  • Formula: Perimeter of a square = 4 x side; Area = side x side.
  • Rectilinear shapes: split into rectangles and add the areas.

lessons.title: Unit 11 Overview - Practical Geometry (textbook page 122)
lessons.notes_html:
Learning Outcomes

Recognise and identify parallel and non-parallel lines. Describe the radius, diameter and circumference of a circle. Recognise and identify acute, right and obtuse angles. Compare and order angles up to 180 degrees by size. Measure and draw angles using a protractor within 180 degrees. Recognise and draw lines of symmetry in 2-D shapes and complete symmetrical figures with respect to a given line of symmetry.

Parallel lines never meet and stay the same distance apart. A circle has a centre, a radius (centre to edge) and a diameter (edge to edge through the centre, twice the radius). Angles are measured in degrees with a protractor: less than 90 degrees is acute, exactly 90 degrees is a right angle, more than 90 degrees is obtuse.

options: Lines that never meet and stay the same distance apart
mcqs.why: The overview states parallel lines never meet and stay the same distance apart, however far they go.

options: Edge to edge through the centre
mcqs.why: The overview defines the radius as centre to edge, while the diameter goes edge to edge through the centre.

mcqs.q: In a circle, what is the diameter?
options: Edge to edge through the centre, twice the radius
The distance around the edge only
mcqs.why: The overview defines the diameter as edge to edge through the centre, and it is twice the radius.

mcqs.q: What instrument is used to measure angles?
mcqs.why: The learning outcomes state angles are measured and drawn using a protractor within 180 degrees.

mcqs.q: An angle less than 90 degrees is called what?
mcqs.why: The overview states less than 90 degrees is acute, exactly 90 degrees is a right angle, more than 90 is obtuse.

mcqs.q: An angle of exactly 90 degrees is called what?
mcqs.why: The overview states exactly 90 degrees is a right angle, less than 90 is acute and more than 90 is obtuse.

mcqs.q: An angle more than 90 degrees is called what?
mcqs.why: The overview states more than 90 degrees is obtuse, exactly 90 degrees is a right angle, less than 90 is acute.

options: The middle point of the circle
mcqs.why: The overview describes a circle as having a centre, with the radius going from the centre to the edge.

mcqs.why: The learning outcomes say to compare and order angles up to 180 degrees and measure and draw within 180 degrees.

options: It is used to complete symmetrical figures
mcqs.why: The outcomes say to recognise lines of symmetry in 2-D shapes and complete symmetrical figures using a given line.

lessons.title: Exercise 11.3
lessons.notes_html:
Method: Angles are measured in degrees with a protractor: place the centre of the protractor on the vertex and the zero line on one arm, then read where the other arm crosses the scale. An angle less than 90 degrees is acute, exactly 90 degrees is a right angle, and more than 90 degrees is obtuse. Note: the printed key gives no values for the measuring item; two angles are exactly 90 degrees (square corner marks) and the other measures are visual estimates marked about, to be checked with a protractor on the printed figure.

Exercise 11.3 - Item 1

(i) Angle MON = 90 degrees, a right angle (it carries the square corner mark).

(ii) Angle GHI is about 105 degrees, an obtuse angle.

(iii) Angle ABC is about 75 degrees, an acute angle.

(iv) Angle JKL is about 135 degrees, an obtuse angle.

(v) Angle TSU = 90 degrees, a right angle (it carries the square corner mark).

(vi) Angle EFG is about 40 degrees, an acute angle. NOTE: the printed key gives no values for this exercise, so the four estimates are marked 'about' and should be checked with a protractor on the printed figure; the two right angles are exact because of their square corner marks.

Exercise 11.3 - Item 2

Exercise 11.3 - Item 3(i)

(i) 30, 60, 45 and 75 degrees;

(ii) 90, 75, 105 and 120 degrees;

(iii) 155, 135, 105, 120 and 90 degrees.

lessons.title: Unit 11 Summary - Practical Geometry
lessons.notes_html:
This summary gathers the main facts of Unit 11: Practical Geometry. Revise these points before a test.

Formula: Diameter = 2 x radius.

lessons.title: Exercise 12.1
lessons.notes_html:
Method: A bar graph shows data as bars. Read the scale first, then read each bar against the scale. To draw a bar graph: label the axes, choose an even scale, and draw one bar per value to its exact height or length. The graphs themselves are drawn by the student; the worked items give the exact data, the construction steps and the interpretation. Note: the printed book lists the 2010 row twice (580 twice); it is one entry and is counted once.

Exercise 12.1 - Item 1

Note: the book lists the 2010 row twice (580 twice); it is a single 2010 entry and is counted once here. Most chairs were sold in 2011 (620) and fewest in 2009 (370). To draw the vertical bar graph: put the years on the horizontal axis and the number of chairs on the vertical axis with a scale of 1 unit = 100 chairs, then draw one bar per year to its height. For the horizontal bar graph: put the years on the vertical axis and the number of chairs on the horizontal axis with the same scale, then draw one bar per year to its length. lessons.title: Exercise 12.2
lessons.notes_html:
Method: Probability words describe chance: impossible means it cannot happen, less likely means a smaller chance, equally likely means the same chance, more likely means a bigger chance, and certain means it must happen. Count the outcomes first, then choose the word that fits. Note: the printed key scrambles the wording in one item and misses out the White Rhinoceros in the review; the worked items give the correct terms and the full list.

Exercise 12.2 - Item 1(i)

(i) Red: 1 out of 4 sections, equally likely.

(ii) Purple: there is no purple section, so it is impossible.

(iii) Any colour: every section has a colour, so it is certain.

Exercise 12.2 - Item 2(i)

(i) Odd numbers are 1, 3 and 5: 3 out of 6 sections, equally likely.

(ii) No number is greater than 6, so it is impossible.

Exercise 12.2 - Item 3(i)

(i) Blue: 1 out of 3, equally likely.

(ii) Yellow: there is no yellow part, so it is impossible.

(iii) All parts red: landing on red is certain.

(iv) Blue: 1 out of 3, less likely than red.

(v) Red: 2 out of 3, more likely than blue.

Exercise 12.2 - Item 4(i)

(i) Less than 4 means 1, 2 or 3: 3 out of 6, equally likely (exactly half). FLAG: the printed key calls this 'more likely', which is incorrect.

(ii) Rolling 7: impossible.

(iii) Getting 1 to 6: every face is 1 to 6, so it is certain. FLAG: the printed key calls this 'equally likely', which is incorrect for the whole set.

(iv) Odd means 1, 3 or 5: 3 out of 6, equally likely. FLAG: the printed key calls this 'more likely', which is incorrect.

(v) Getting 3 is 1 out of 6, while getting an odd number is 3 out of 6, so getting 3 is less likely.

lessons.title: Glossary - Terms and Meanings (textbook page 162)
lessons.notes_html:
The Glossary (textbook page 162) is a word list, not an exercise, so it has no solved items. The terms below are summarised from the book Glossary for quick revision.

TermMeaning
Place ValueIt is the value of a digit based on its position in a number.
RoundingRounding is the process of replacing a number with a simpler, approximate value that is closest to it.
Roman NumbersRoman numbers are a numeral system that uses letters from the Latin alphabet (I, V, X, L, C, D, M) to represent numbers.
Expanded formWriting a number as the sum of the place value of its digits, is called its Expanded form.
Ascending orderIt means arranging numbers from the smallest to the largest.
Descending orderIt means arranging numbers from the largest to the smallest.
RegroupingIt is the process of rearranging numbers by carrying over or borrowing to make addition or subtraction easier.
MinuendThe number from which another number is subtracted.
SubtrahendThe number that is to be subtracted.
DifferenceThe result obtained after subtraction.
SumIt is the result obtained after adding two or more numbers.
EstimateIt is an approximate calculation of a number or result, often by rounding.
DivisorThe number that divides another number.
DividendThe number being divided.
QuotientThe result obtained after division.
RemainderThe number left over after division.
FactorsNumbers that exactly divide another number without remainder.
MultiplesNumbers obtained by multiplying a given number by whole numbers.
Prime NumbersNumbers greater than 1 having only two factors, 1 and itself.
Composite NumbersNumbers greater than 1 having more than two factors.
FractionA number that represents a part of a whole.
Proper FractionA fraction in which the numerator is smaller than the denominator.
Improper FractionA fraction in which the numerator is greater than or equal to the denominator.
Mixed NumbersA number made up of a whole number and a fraction.
Like FractionsFractions with the same denominator.
Unlike FractionsFractions with different denominators.
DecimalsNumbers expressed using a decimal point to show parts of a whole.
Decimal PlacesThe number of digits to the right of the decimal point.
TenthsOne part when a whole is divided into ten equal parts.
HundredthsOne part when a whole is divided into one hundred equal parts.
ThousandthsOne part when a whole is divided into one thousand equal parts.
QuarterOne part when a whole is divided into four equal parts.
HalfOne of two equal parts of a whole.
Three-QuarterThree parts out of four equal parts of a whole.
Increasing PatternA sequence where numbers or objects grow in value or size.
Decreasing PatternA sequence where numbers or objects reduce in value or size.
Number SentenceA mathematical statement with numbers and symbols.
ExpressionA combination of numbers and operations without an equal sign.
Parallel LinesLines that never meet and are always the same distance apart.
Non-parallel LinesLines that are not always the same distance apart and may meet.
RadiusThe distance from the center of a circle to any point on its circumference.
DiameterA line passing through the center of a circle, touching both ends of its circumference.
CircumferenceThe distance around a circle.
Acute AngleAn angle smaller than 90 degrees.
Right AngleAn angle exactly equal to 90 degrees.
Obtuse AngleAn angle greater than 90 degrees but less than 180 degrees.
Line of SymmetryA line that divides a figure into two equal mirror-image parts.
Symmetrical FiguresFigures that can be divided into two equal mirror-image halves.
Bar GraphA graph that uses bars to represent data.
ProbabilityThe chance or likelihood of an event happening.

lessons.title: Notes on the Printed Book - Corrections and Flags
lessons.notes_html:
This page records every place where these notes differ from the printed book, and why. Nothing was invented to fill a gap.

Coverage: what these notes cover.

These notes cover all numbered exercises and all review exercises in Units 1 to 12 of Mathematics-420, the complete book. In-text Activities are classroom tasks (group work, measuring and drawing in class), distinct from the numbered exercises; they are not written out as solved items, and the student does the activity in class. The Glossary (printed page 162) is a word list, not an exercise, so it has no solved items.

Printed-book errors corrected in these notes (the correct mathematics is given in the exercise itself).

Unit 1: the printed key says 13,076 is less than 10,772 (it is greater); worked Example 7 swaps the ascending and descending labels; the Roman table misprints XLII as 41 (correct 42); the words key gives 'Fifty thousand and one' for 50,006 (correct 'Fifty thousand and six'). Unit 5: the 'Remember!' box shows 7/3 as 2 2/8 with divisor 8 (correct 2 1/3, divisor 3). Unit 6: the worked examples swap 427/100 and 4321/1000 (correct 4.27 and 4.321); the key misprints 9.47 + 51.5 as 6.97 (correct 60.97) and 43.5 + 3.32 as 46.80 (correct 46.82). Review 4: the key marks 986 divisible by 3 (digit sum 23, so it is not). Review 9: the key gives 10:45 a.m. for 22:45 (correct 10:45 p.m.) and 100 seconds for 3 minutes 10 seconds (correct 190 seconds). Review 10: the key gives 5,956 cm squared for 124 x 44 (correct 5,456). Exercise 11.4 Question 2: the key garbles two angles as 10 degrees and 90 degrees (the question's 20 degrees and 130 degrees are used). Probability wording in the printed key is scrambled in places (Exercise 12.2 Question 4 and Review 12 Question 1 part (e), which omits the White Rhinoceros); the mathematically correct terms and the full list are given.

Printed-book misprints flagged, not silently fixed.

Exercise 5.5 Question 1 part (x): the first factor is missing in print (the box starts with a multiplication sign); only the printed part is worked (7 5/41 x 11 = 78 14/41) and nothing is guessed. Exercise 5.6 Question 4: the question prints '2' followed by a gap before 'pizzas'; it is solved as 2 pizzas (1/2 pizza each for 4 friends) and the gap is flagged. Exercise 7.2 Question 3 part (ii): the printed '20' breaks the +4 pattern (the next term should be 22). Exercise 12.1 Question 1: the 2010 row is printed twice (580 twice) and is counted once. Review 8 Question 4: the book prints 'millilitre (mm)' where millimetre is meant. Review 8 Question 9: the book prints 'for' where 'four' is meant. Exercise 6.7 Question 3: the book says 'rice' where wheat is meant.

Estimates, not exact key values.

Exercise 11.3 Question 1: the printed key gives no values at all for this exercise. Two angles are exactly 90 degrees (square corner marks). The other four measures (about 105, 75, 135 and 40 degrees) are visual estimates and are marked 'about'; check them with a protractor on the printed figure.

Graphs and drawings.

Bar graphs (Exercise 12.1 Questions 1 and 2, Review 12 Questions 2 and 3) and protractor drawings and mirror images (Exercise 11.3 Question 3, Exercise 11.4 Question 2, Exercise 11.5 Questions 2 and 3) must be drawn by the student: this notes builder draws vector shapes only, not data bar charts or protractor figures. Each such item therefore gives the exact data, the construction steps and the interpretation, so the student can draw it correctly.

mcqs.q: What do these notes cover, according to the corrections page?
options: All numbered and review exercises in Units 1 to 12
mcqs.why: The page states these notes cover all numbered exercises and all review exercises in Units 1 to 12.

mcqs.q: What are in-text Activities, according to the page?
options: Classroom tasks done by the student in class
mcqs.why: The page states Activities are classroom tasks, distinct from numbered exercises, done by the student in class.

mcqs.q: The Glossary is on which printed page and what is it?
options: Page 162, a word list with no solved items
mcqs.why: The page states the Glossary (printed page 162) is a word list, not an exercise, so it has no solved items.

mcqs.q: What is the correct value of the Roman numeral XLII, correcting the misprint?
mcqs.why: Step 1: The page states the Roman table misprints XLII as 41; the correct value is 42, as corrected here.

mcqs.q: What are the correct words for 50,006, correcting the key?
mcqs.why: Step 1: The page states the key gives Fifty thousand and one for 50,006; correct is Fifty thousand and six.

mcqs.q: What is 7/3 as a mixed number, correcting the Unit 5 box?
mcqs.why: Step 1: 7 divided by 3 = 2 remainder 1, so 7/3 = 2 1/3 with divisor 3, correcting the printed 2 2/8.

mcqs.q: What is 9.47 + 51.5, correcting the Unit 6 key?
mcqs.why: Step 1: 9.47 + 51.5 = 60.97. The page states the key misprints this as 6.97; 60.97 is correct.

mcqs.q: Why is 986 NOT divisible by 3, according to the page?
options: Its digit sum is 23, so it is not divisible by 3
mcqs.why: Step 1: Digit sum = 9 + 8 + 6 = 23, which is not divisible by 3, so 986 is not divisible by 3.

mcqs.q: What is 22:45 in 12-hour time, correcting Review 9?
mcqs.why: Step 1: 22:45 is in the evening, so it is 10:45 p.m., correcting the key value of 10:45 a.m. in Review 9.

mcqs.q: How many seconds are in 3 minutes 10 seconds, correcting Review 9?
mcqs.why: Step 1: 3 minutes = 3 x 60 = 180 seconds. Step 2: 180 + 10 = 190 seconds, correcting the key value 100.
